passage:
On Saturday afternoon Nandini and her brother Akash both grabbed the TV remote. "My turn!" "No, mine!" Their voices rose until Amma walked in. "One show each. Put the timer on my phone." Nandini took the first turn, and when the timer rang she handed the remote over without a scuffle.

At school, her friends only talked about a new online game, and Nandini felt lonely when she did not join. That evening she played for hours with them, and afterwards her eyes hurt and her head felt fuzzy. Amma, whose name was Irawati, noticed. "You look tired, darling. Are you sleeping okay?" Nandini flared. "You are always staring at my screen!" Then she saw her mother's worried face. "You are worried, not mean," she said. Together they agreed on a limit: screens off by eight.

On Sunday she invited two friends to play cricket downstairs, and one said, "Actually, good idea."

Dada watched from his chair. "You children never talk to me anymore. Everyone is on a phone." Nandini's stomach dropped. She put her phone in a drawer and sat beside him. "Tell me a story, Dada." He told her about riding a bicycle to school with a goat chasing him, and they both laughed until dinner.

qa.q: What did Dada tell Nandini a story about?
qa.a: He told her about riding a bicycle to school with a goat chasing him.

qa.q: How did the way Nandini settled the remote quarrel differ from how she first reacted when Irawati noticed she was tired?
qa.a: With Akash, one show each and a timer settled it without shouting. With Irawati she flared until she saw her mother's worried face, then agreed on a limit together. With Dada she put her phone away for a story.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when Dada said the children never talk to him?
qa.a: She felt guilty. Her stomach dropped and she put her phone in a drawer.

qa.q: What could Nandini do about friends who only want to play online?
qa.a: She could invite them to play outdoors, as she did with cricket, and notice how she feels after long screen time.

grounding: Screen time shows up as a quarrel over the remote, friends who only play online, a mother's worry about tiredness, and a grandfather's wish to talk.

passage:
Tarun's hostel room was quiet at eleven when Sumit's message came: "Say I was at your place on Saturday." Tarun typed back, "I will keep your private plans private. I won't lie about where you were, and I won't cover for the night races. Tell Papa yourself." Sumit sulked for a day, then said okay.

Over the holidays Papa praised Uday's new job at every meal, and Tarun felt a sour tightness. He did not slam any doors. He told Amma, "I know Uday is doing well. It hurts a bit when I feel invisible." Amma blinked. "We should ask about your projects." That evening they did.

Uday, meanwhile, drove Papa to every check-up and handled the bank paperwork without complaint. Tarun noticed the tiredness on his face. "You are carrying more than me. Let us split it. I will take the paperwork on weekends and call the clinic." Uday exhaled. "Thanks. I was keeping count in my head."

Back at the hostel, Tarun called both brothers on video. "I did not realise how much I lean on you two. Thank you." Sumit made a face and said, "Weirdo." Uday just grinned.

qa.q: What did Tarun offer to take on for Uday?
qa.a: He offered to take the paperwork on weekends and call the clinic.

qa.q: How did Tarun's handling of Sumit's request differ from his handling of Uday's load of care?
qa.a: With Sumit he kept private plans private but would not lie or hide the night races. With Uday he had an honest talk and split the duties before the silent counting could blow up.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when Papa praised Uday's job at every meal?
qa.a: He felt a sour tightness of jealousy and felt invisible.

qa.q: What helped Tarun with his envy of Uday?
qa.a: He told Amma how it felt instead of sabotaging Uday, and Amma agreed to ask about his projects.

grounding: Adult siblings meet a request to cover, envy of a favoured brother, unequal care duties, and a moment of open thanks across distance.

passage:
Before the maths test, Sarita leaned across. "Let me see what you wrote for number four. Friends help each other, right?" Lalremsiami's tummy tightened. She did not want to lose a friend, and she did not want trouble. "No," she said. "But I will help you study after school." Sarita huffed and turned away.

During the test Sarita's eyes drifted toward Lakshmi's paper. Her heart banged, and each time the teacher's shoes squeaked she froze. She asked herself: if nobody would ever know, would I still do this? She turned back to her own page.

Lakshmi had copied a sum the week before and slipped by unnoticed, but the unease sat in her like a stone. After the test she stayed behind. "I copied a sum last week. I am sorry, and I will not do it again."

Lalremsiami had noticed Lakshmi too, and felt superior. At lunch she whispered it to three girls, and their laughter felt sour. That night she saw that she had not helped anyone. She had only spread a story. Her anger at cheating was fair, but next time she would tell the teacher quietly, if it was needed.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami offer Sarita instead of her answers?
qa.a: She offered to help Sarita study after school.

qa.q: How did Sarita's and Lakshmi's uneasy feelings differ from Lalremsiami's, and what did each do?
qa.a: Sarita feared being caught and asked what she would do if nobody found out, then turned back to her own page. Lakshmi's unease over a copied sum led her to admit it and promise not to repeat it. Lalremsiami said no kindly, but then felt superior and whispered about Lakshmi, which helped nobody.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling after she copied a sum the week before?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and guilty, like a stone sitting inside her.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami do next time she notices someone cheating?
qa.a: She could tell the teacher quietly, if it is needed, instead of gossiping to classmates.

grounding: Around one test, a friend's request for answers, fear of being caught, a classmate's uneasy conscience after copying, and another's gossip show different stances on cheating.

passage:
When the doctor said the word, Jasleen's ears rang. On the way home she was terrified: for her parents, for her future, for everything. That night she searched online until 3 a.m., and her fear grew with each page. By morning she stopped and wrote a list of questions instead.

Her friend Seema came to the next appointment and took notes. The doctor explained the options plainly, including what was not yet known, and answered each question twice when needed. "If anything is unclear, ask again," they said. Jasleen liked being told the truth. She shared her full history and asked for a second opinion, and the doctor did not mind.

At home, a hot wave of anger rose. "Why me? I am twenty-five!" She snapped at Siddharth over the wrong tea, then apologised. Later she went for a fast walk and filled three pages in a notebook, letting the bitterness out.

On Sundays her prayer group came to sing, and the songs held her. She also kept every appointment and followed the plan. When a stranger offered a miracle cure in place of treatment, she said no.

qa.q: Until what time did Jasleen search online that night?
qa.a: She searched online until 3 a.m.

qa.q: How did Jasleen's late-night searching differ from the appointment with Seema, and how did faith fit with her treatment?
qa.a: Late-night searching fed her fear. Bringing Seema, writing questions and hearing the options plainly let her take it in stages. The songs of her prayer group comforted her while she still followed the plan.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she snapped at Siddharth over the wrong tea?
qa.a: She felt angry and bitter, asking why this had happened to her at twenty-five.

qa.q: What helped Jasleen with her anger without hurting the people around her?
qa.a: She apologised, then went for a fast walk and filled three pages in a notebook to let the bitterness out.

grounding: After a serious diagnosis one person meets fear, a doctor who explains honestly, anger at the unfairness, and comfort from a prayer group beside treatment.

passage:
When the cousins gathered at Nani's house, two older ones, Meena and Kabir, ran off to the terrace and shut the door on Jeevan. It stung. He knocked and asked, "Can I come and play too?" When they said, "Later," he suggested carrom on the porch and found Ira willing.

Ira was quick at cricket and at sums, and Jeevan wanted to beat her at both. He bowled his hardest, and when she hit a six he groaned. But then he noticed the twist of her wrist and asked how she did it. She showed him, laughing, and they played until the light dimmed.

At tea, an aunt said, "Ira got such good marks. And Jeevan? Try to be like her." Jeevan's ears burned and he felt small. That night he told Amma, "It hurts when they compare me. I am not a number." Amma hugged him. "I will speak to Aunty." Ira, nearby, looked down at her plate, as though she felt judged too.

On Sunday some boys from the lane began teasing little Chinmay about his lisp. Jeevan walked over and stood beside him. "Leave him alone," he said quietly. When they did not stop, he went to fetch Chinmay's father.

qa.q: What game did Jeevan suggest to Ira on the porch?
qa.a: He suggested carrom.

qa.q: How did Jeevan deal with being left out and with the comparison, and how was his rivalry with Ira different from the marks talk?
qa.a: He asked to join and then suggested another game, so being left out ended in carrom. The rivalry with Ira turned into learning her wrist twist, while the comparison of marks stung and he told Amma how it hurt.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when the aunt told him to be like Ira?
qa.a: He felt small and hurt. His ears burned.

qa.q: How did Jeevan help little Chinmay when the boys teased him?
qa.a: He stood beside Chinmay, spoke calmly, and fetched an adult when they did not stop.

grounding: A cousins' gathering brings exclusion, friendly rivalry, comparison of marks in front of relatives, and protecting a small cousin from teasing.

passage:
Gurleen had hidden a laptop instalment plan from Saurabh for two months, sure he would sulk. When the second bill arrived, she sat him down. "I bought it without telling you, and I am sorry. Here is a plan to pay it off by December." Saurabh took a deep breath. He was hurt more by the hiding than by the amount. They wrote the plan on the fridge whiteboard.

Saurabh was between jobs, retraining for a data course, and Gurleen paid most of the bills. She felt protective and heavy at once. Instead of sighing, she said, "Let us list what you would like to earn, and by when." They made a schedule with milestones and no jokes about freeloading.

Saurabh, for his part, felt he owed her everything, since she had paid his fees. He told his friend Hrithik, "I feel I cannot disagree with her now." Hrithik said, "Say thanks by helping at home, and still say what you think." That night Saurabh said, "I am grateful. And I would like us to choose the sofa together."

A silent resentment had also been growing in Gurleen about the money sent to Saurabh's parents each month. She said so aloud, kindly. "It is a lot, and I never told you." They agreed on an amount together and stopped keeping the ledger in their heads.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen and Saurabh write down the plan?
qa.a: They wrote it on the fridge whiteboard.

qa.q: How did Gurleen's hidden bill differ from her open talk about Saurabh's job and the money sent to his parents?
qa.a: Hiding the bill hurt trust more than the amount, and she repaired it by confessing with a plan. Talking openly about milestones and the money for his parents kept resentment from growing in silence and made both matters shared decisions.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when he told Hrithik he could not disagree with Gurleen now?
qa.a: He felt indebted and worried that his own voice was shrinking because she had paid his fees.

qa.q: What did Hrithik suggest Saurabh do about the feeling of owing her?
qa.a: He suggested saying thanks by helping at home while still saying what he thinks.

grounding: One couple faces a hidden purchase, a partner who depends on the other's income, a debt of gratitude, and a quiet resentment over money sent to parents.
